title: Remark
body_md: \cite{shaer23a} observed as a practical consideration that derandomizing the dummy variable $\widetilde{X}$ when constructing antisymmetric e-variables can improve power. This is because derandomization effectively leads to a different null hypothesis, as discussed later in Section \ref{sect:null_intermediate} and Appendix \ref{appendix:hypotheses}. Nevertheless, the comparison results that follow remain unchanged when this derandomization is incorporated into the analysis.

label: thm:small_signal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:small_signal}
Assume that the signal strength $\Delta$ is sufficiently small. Define
               
\[
\sigma_0^2 := \mathbb{V}(l(m(\widetilde {X},Z),Y)),
\qquad
\sigma_1^2 := \mathbb{V}(l(m(X,Z),Y)).
\]

Then, up to second order in $\Delta$, the optimal parameters for the exponential and coin-betting e-values satisfy

\begin{align*}
    \eta^\star
=
\frac{\Delta}{\sigma_0^2}
+
O(\Delta^2),\qquad
\lambda^\star
=
\frac{\Delta}{\sigma_1^2+\Delta^2}
+
O(\Delta^2).
\end{align*}

Moreover, the corresponding optimal  e-powers satisfy
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log E_{\exp}^{\eta^\star}\right]
&=
\frac{\Delta^2}{2\sigma_0^2}
+
O(\Delta^3), \\
    \mathbb{E}\!\left[\log E_{\mathrm{cb}}^{\lambda^\star}\right]
&=
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\Delta^2}{\sigma_1^2+\Delta^2}
+
O(\Delta^3).
\end{align*}

label: prop:double_robust
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:double_robust}
Let $K_n(\cdot\mid Z)$ be an $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable estimate of $K(\cdot\mid Z)$, and suppose that, conditionally on $(\mathcal F_{n-1},Z)$, the random variables $X$ and $\widetilde X'_n$ have distributions $K(\cdot\mid Z)$ and $K_n(\cdot\mid Z)$, respectively.
Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (i)] \textbf{Lipschitz convergence.} Suppose that, uniformly in $z, y$, $|r_n(x,z,y)-r_n(x',z,y)| \leq b_n(z,y)\,|x-x'|$ for some $b_n$. Define $a_n(Z) := \mathcal W_1(K_n(\cdot\mid Z), K(\cdot\mid Z))$. Then, for every $z, y$,
   
    $\left|\mathbb E_{K_n}[r_n(\widetilde X_n,z,y)] - \mathbb E_{K}[r_n(X,z,y)]\right| \leq a_n b_n.$
   

\item[\rm (ii)] \textbf{Uniform convergence.} Suppose that $\sup_{x,z,y}|r_n(x,z,y)| \leq b_n(z,y)$ for some $b_n$. Define $a_n(Z) := \mathrm d_{\mathrm{TV}}(K_n(\cdot\mid Z), K(\cdot\mid Z))$. Then, for every $z, y$,
$
    \left|\mathbb E_{K_n}[r_n(\widetilde X_n,z,y)] - \mathbb E_{K}[r_n(X,z,y)]\right| \leq 2a_nb_n.
$

\item[\rm (iii)] \textbf{$L_2$ convergence.} Suppose that $\mathbb E_{K}[r_n(X,Z,Y)^2 \mid \mathcal F_{n-1}] \leq b_n^2$ for some $b_n$. Define $a_n := \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm d_{\chi^2}(K_n(\cdot\mid Z) \Vert K(\cdot\mid Z))^2\right]}$. Then
$
    \left|\mathbb E[r_n(\widetilde X_n',Z,Y) - r_n(X,Z,Y)]\right| \leq a_nb_n.
$
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Double robustness

label: thm:antisymmetric_type_I
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:antisymmetric_type_I}
Assume any of the three scenarios from Proposition~\ref{prop:double_robust} hold. Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ be the corresponding distributional and model-convergence rates, and let $\delta_n$ denote the corresponding failure probability $A_n$.
 
Then, for $P\in\mathcal{P}_{K}^\textnormal{X-CI}$,

$$
\mathbb E_P[E_n \mathds{1}_{A_n}\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]
\leq
1+\lambda a_nb_n.
$$

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P &
\left(
\sup_{1\leq n\leq N}
E^{(n)}
\geq \frac{1}{\alpha}
\right)
-\alpha
\\&\leq
\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_n
+
\alpha
\left[
\exp\left(
\lambda\sum_{n=1}^N a_nb_n
\right)-1
\right].
\end{align*}

body_md:
Assume that the loss is given by the $0$--$1$ loss. Then, the optimal value of $\lambda$ maximizing the coin-betting e-value is
\[
\lambda_\star
=
\frac{p_1-p_0}{p_0(1-p_0)}.
\]

Similarly, the optimal $\eta$ for the exponential e-value \eqref{eq:exp_def} is
\[
\eta_\star
=
\log\!\left(
\frac{p_0(1-p_1)}{p_1(1-p_0)}
\right).
\]

With these choices, both e-values coincide and are given by
\[
E^{\eta_\star}_{\mathrm{exp}}
=
E^{\lambda_\star}_{\mathrm{cb}}
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1-p_1}{1-p_0},
& m(X,Z)=Y, \\[1.2ex]
\dfrac{p_1}{p_0},
& m(X,Z)\neq Y.
\end{cases}
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that the e-power of the exponential e-value, denoted by $\mathcal{P}_{\exp}^{\eta}$, is given by
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\exp}^{\eta}
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\!\left(E_{\exp}^{\eta}\right)\right]
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
-\eta\, l(m(X,Z),Y)
-
\log
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
\right].
\]

Recall that the inner expectation is formally taken with respect to
\(P_{\widetilde X\mid X,Y,Z}\). However, since
\(\widetilde X \perp\!\!\!\perp (X,Y)\mid Z\), we simply write
\(P_{\widetilde X\mid Z}\) to avoid cumbersome notation.

Define
\[
\psi(\eta)
:=
\log
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right].
\]

Using a Taylor expansion around \(\eta=0\),
\[
\psi(\eta)
=
\psi(0)
+
\eta \psi'(0)
+
\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\psi''(0)
+
O(\eta^{3}).
\]

Since
\[
\psi(0)
=
\log
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}[1]
=
0,
\]
we have
\[
\psi(0)=0.
\]

Differentiating,
\[
\psi'(\eta)
=
-\frac{
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
}{
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
},
\]
and therefore
\[
\psi'(0)
=
-\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right].
\]

Differentiating once more yields
\begin{align*}
\psi''(\eta)
&=
\frac{
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)^2
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
\,
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
}{
\left(
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
\right)^2
}
\\
&\qquad
-
\frac{
\left(
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
\right)^2
}{
\left(
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
e^{-\eta l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)}
\right]
\right)^2
}.
\end{align*}

Evaluating at \(\eta=0\), we obtain
\begin{align*}
\psi''(0)
&=
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)^2
\right]
-
\left(
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right]
\right)^2
\\
&=
\operatorname{Var}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left(
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right)
\\
&=:
\sigma_0^2.
\end{align*}

Substituting the Taylor expansion into the e-power expression gives
\begin{align*}
\mathcal P_{\exp}^{\eta}
&=
-\eta\,
\mathbb E\!\left[l(m(X,Z),Y)\right]
\\
&\qquad
-
\mathbb E\!\left[
-\eta\,
\mathbb E_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left[
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right]
+
\frac{\eta^2}{2}\,
\operatorname{Var}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left(
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right)
+
O(\eta^3)
\right]
\\
&=
-\eta
\Bigl(
\mathbb E[l(m(X,Z),Y)]
-
\mathbb E\bigl[
\mathbb E_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
[l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)]
\bigr]
\Bigr)
\\
&\qquad
-
\frac{\eta^2}{2}\,
\mathbb E
\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left(
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right)
\right]
+
O(\eta^3).
\end{align*}

Recall that
\[
\Delta
:=
\mathbb E\bigl[l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\bigr]
-
\mathbb E[l(m(X,Z),Y)]
\]
and
\[
\sigma_0^2
:=
\mathbb E
\!\left[
\operatorname{Var}_{\widetilde X\mid Z}
\!\left(
l(m(\widetilde X,Z),Y)
\right)
\right].
\]

Then
\[
\mathcal P_{\exp}^{\eta}
=
\eta \Delta
-
\frac{\eta^2}{2}\sigma_0^2
+
O(\eta^3).
\]

Ignoring higher-order terms and maximizing the quadratic approximation yields
\[
\eta^*
=
\frac{\Delta}{\sigma_0^2},
\]
and
\[
\mathcal P_{\exp}^*
=
\frac{\Delta^2}{2\sigma_0^2}.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall that the coin-betting e-value is given by
\[
E_{\mathrm{cb}}^\lambda
=
1
-
\lambda\!\left(
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(X,Z),Y\right)
-
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}\!\left[
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(\widetilde X,Z),Y\right)
\right]
\right),
\]
where the expectation is taken only over $\widetilde{X}$ condition both on $Z$ and $Y$, but for simplicity, and to underline that $\widetilde{X}$ is independent of $Y$, we hide this conditioning on $Y$.
Its e-power is
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cb}}^\lambda
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\!\left(E_{\mathrm{cb}}^\lambda\right)\right]
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\log\!\left(
1
-
\lambda\!\left(
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(X,Z),Y\right)
-
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}\!\left[
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(\widetilde X,Z),Y\right)
\right]
\right)
\right)
\right].
\]

Using the Taylor expansion
\[
\log(1+x)
=
x-\frac{x^2}{2}+O(x^3),
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cb}}^\lambda
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\lambda D
+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^2 D^2
\right]
+
O(\lambda^3),
\]
where
\[
D
:=
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}\!\left[
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(\widetilde X,Z),Y\right)
\right]-
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(X,Z),Y\right).
\]

Recall that the predictiveness signal is
\[
\Delta
:=
\mathbb{E}[D]
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde X \mid Z}\!\left[
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(\widetilde X,Z),Y\right)
\right]
\right]
-
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
l\!\left(\widehat{m}(X,Z),Y\right)
\right],
\]
and define
\[
\sigma_1'^2
:=
\mathbb{E}[D^2].
\]

Then
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cb}}^\lambda
=
\lambda \Delta
-
\frac{1}{2}\lambda^2 \sigma_1'^2
+
O(\lambda^3).
\]

Ignoring higher-order terms, the optimal value of $\lambda$ is obtained by maximizing the quadratic approximation, yielding
\[
\lambda^*
=
\frac{\Delta}{\sigma_1'^2}.
\]

Substituting this value back gives
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cb}}^*
=
\frac{\Delta^2}{2\sigma_1'^2}.
\]

We conclude by noting that $\sigma_1'^2=\sigma_1^2+\Delta^2$.

body_md:
Indeed, for any e-variable \(E=h(t,\widetilde t)\), we have
\begin{align*}
h(t,\widetilde t)
&=
\frac12\bigl(h(t,\widetilde t)+h(\widetilde t,t)\bigr)
+
\frac12\bigl(h(t,\widetilde t)-h(\widetilde t,t)\bigr).
\end{align*}

The second term is antisymmetric. Moreover, for all $t$ and $\widetilde t$ the following is in the null hypothesis,
\[
P=\frac12\bigl(\delta_{t,\widetilde t}+\delta_{\widetilde t,t}\bigr),
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac12\bigl(h(t,\widetilde t)+h(\widetilde t,t)\bigr)\le 1.
\]
Verifying that $1 + \frac12\bigl(h(t,\widetilde t)-h(\widetilde t,t)\bigr)$ is an e-variable proves the claim.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof consists of a change-of-measure argument similar to that in~\citet{numeraire}. Indeed, denoting by $f_{T, \widetilde{T}}$ the density under the alternative $Q$ and by $\tilde{P}$ the measure with density
\[
p(T,\widetilde{T}) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(T,\widetilde{T}) + f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(\widetilde{T},T)\bigr)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(T,\widetilde{T}) > 0\}},
\]
we obtain 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_Q\!\left[\frac{E}{E^\star}\right]
&= \mathbb{E}_Q\!\left[
\frac{1 + g(T,\widetilde{T})}
{\frac{f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(T,\widetilde{T})}{\frac{1}{2}\bigl(f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(T,\widetilde{T}) + f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(\widetilde{T},T)\bigr)}}
\right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}}\!\left[(1 + g(T,\widetilde{T}))\,
\mathbf{1}_{\{f_{T, \widetilde{T}}(T,\widetilde{T}) > 0\}}\right] \\
&\le \mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}}\!\left[1 + g(T,\widetilde{T})\right]
= 1.
\end{align*}

Note that there is no need for $E$ to be of the form $1+g$, since, by the very definition of an e-value, we have $\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}}[E]\leq 1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
$E^{\text{cond exch}}_B$ is an e-variable for $\mathcal{P}^{\text{cond exch}}_{B+1}$, while $E^{\text{cond exch}}_{B+1}$ is the GRO e-variable for the same null, and thus has a greater or equal e-power. Therefore, the e-power sequence weakly grows. Furthermore, in Section \ref{sect:limiting_gro_cond_exch}, we have seen that the limiting e-variable is the conditional likelihood ratio
\begin{equation*}
    E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_{\infty} = \frac{f_{T|Y,Z}(T|Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(T|Y,Z)}.
\end{equation*}
Note that 
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}_Q\left[\ln\left(E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B\right)\right] \leq \mathbb{E}_{Q(Y,Z)}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\left(Q(T|Y,Z) || Q(\widetilde{T}|Y,Z)\right)\right]
\end{equation*}
must hold for all $B$. This is true because $\mathcal{P}^{\textnormal{PFX-CI}}_{K^{\#}}$ can always be equivalently represented (similar to Section \ref{sect:proof_mx_as_cond_exch} ) by adding $B$ conditionally independent dummy variables $\widetilde{T}_i \sim K^{\#}_{Y,Z}$ with same distribution under the alternative, and making the same exchangeability requirements as in $\mathcal{P}^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B$. The addition of dummy variables does not change the GRO e-variable, but makes it immediately clear that $\mathcal{P}^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B$ is a larger null hypothesis, and thus has a weaker GRO e-variable.
\\
What remains is to show that the e-power gap tends to $0$. Fatou's lemma implies:
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_{\infty})^+\right] \leq \lim \inf_B \mathbb{E}\left[(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B)^+\right].
\end{equation*}
If we can further show that $(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B)^-$ is a uniformly integrable sequence, we will have
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_{\infty})^-\right] = \lim_B \mathbb{E}\left[(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B)^-\right]
\end{equation*}
and the proof will be finished by subtracting this equality from Fatou's inequality. The rest of the proof is devoted to showing uniform integrability indeed holds.\\
Note that
\[
E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B = \frac{\frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}}{M_B}, \text{ with }
\qquad
M_B = \frac{1}{B+1}\left(\frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}
+ \sum_{i=1}^{B} \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}\right).
\]
Since
\[
\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B = \ln \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)} - \ln M_B,
\]
we have
\[
\big(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B\big)^- \le \left(\ln \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}\right)^- + (\ln M_B)^+ .
\]
Define
\[
A_B = \frac{1}{B+1}\sum_{i=1}^{B} \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
M_B \le \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)} + A_B .
\]
Using $\ln^+(a+b) \le \ln 2 + \ln^+ a + \ln^+ b$ and $\ln^+ x \le x$, we obtain
\[
\big(\ln E^{\textnormal{cond exch}}_B\big)^- \le \left|\ln \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}\right| + \ln 2 + A_B .
\]
It therefore suffices to show that the right-hand side is uniformly integrable in $B$.

\emph{The term $A_B$.} Since $\widetilde{T}_1,\dots,\widetilde{T}_B$ are i.i.d.\ given $(Y,Z)$, the pairs $(\widetilde{T}_i,(Y,Z))$ share a common law, so the variables
\[
\frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}, \qquad i \ge 1,
\]
are identically distributed. They are nonnegative with
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(\widetilde{T}_i\mid Y,Z)} \,\middle|\, Y,Z\right]
= \int f_{T\mid Y,Z}(t\mid Y,Z)\,\mathrm{d}t = 1 .
\]
An identically distributed family of integrable variables is uniformly integrable, and so is the family of its averages. Thus, $\{A_B\}_{B\ge 1}$ is uniformly integrable.

\emph{The term involving $T$.} This is a single random variable, so it suffices that it is integrable under $f$. For the negative part, using $\ln x \leq x$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\ln \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}\right)^- \,\middle|\, Y,Z\right]
\le \int_{\{t:f_{T\mid Y,Z}(t|Y,Z) < f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(t|Y,Z)\}} f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(t\mid Y,Z) \mathrm{d}t \leq 1 .
\]
For the positive part, integrability holds if and only if
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\ln \frac{f_{T\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}{f_{\widetilde{T}\mid Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)}\right]
< \infty,
\]
which is true by assumption.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:gro_for_exch_limit}
Suppose that under the point alternative $Q(\widetilde{T}^{\infty}, T, Y, Z)$, $\{\widetilde{T}_i\}_i, T$ are all independent given $Y,Z$, and $\{\widetilde{T}_i\}_i$ are further conditionally identically distributed. Furthermore, distributions $Q(T| Y, Z), Q(\widetilde{T}| Y, Z) , Q(Y, Z)$ are given by (conditional) densities $f_{T|Y,Z}, f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}, f_{Y,Z}$ respectively, and $(Y,Z)$ takes values in a compact subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$.
Write $w(t\mid y,z) \overset{def}{=} f_{T|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)/f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)$ for the likelihood ratio (with $0/0=0$), and $\varphi(y,z) \overset{def}{=}  Q(\widetilde{T} \in \cdot|Y=y,Z=z)$.
Under the regularity assumptions
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{(Continuity and upper bound)}
          For every $t$, the maps $(y,z) \mapsto f_{T|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)$ and
          $(y,z) \mapsto f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)$ are continuous, and there
          exists a constant $C < \infty$ s.t.
          $f_{T|Y,Z}(t \mid y,z), f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(t \mid y,z) \le C$ for all $t,y,z$.
 
    \item \textbf{(Lipschitz likelihood ratio)}
          $f_{T|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)=0$ whenever $f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)=0$, and there is a function $L(t)\ge0$ such that for all $t,y,z,y',z'$,
          \[
              \bigl|w(t\mid y,z)-w(t\mid y',z')\bigr| \le L(t)||(y,z) - (y',z')||,
          \]
          and $\ell(y,z)\overset{def}{=}\int L(t)\, f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)\,dt<\infty$ for all $y,z$.
 
    \item \textbf{(Posterior consistency)}
          $Q(\widetilde{T}^\infty,Y,Z)$-a.s.,
          \[
              f_{Y,Z\mid \widetilde{T}^B}(\cdot,\cdot \mid \widetilde{T}^B)
              \xrightarrow{w} \Pi_{\varphi(Y,Z)}
              \quad \text{as } B \to \infty,
          \]
          where $\Pi_{\varphi(Y,Z)}$ is a probability measure supported on the
          fiber $\varphi^{-1}(\{\varphi(Y,Z)\})$.
\end{enumerate}
the limiting e-variable for conditional exchangeability is $Q(\widetilde{T}^\infty, T ,Y,Z)$-a.s.\ given by
\begin{equation*}
 \lim _{B \to \infty}E_B^{\textnormal{exch}}(T,\widetilde{T}^B) = \frac{f_{T|\varphi(Y,Z)}(T\mid\varphi(Y,Z))}{  f_{\widetilde{T}|Y,Z}(T\mid Y,Z)},
\end{equation*}
where
$f_{T|\varphi(Y,Z)}(t\mid\varphi(Y,Z)) \overset{def}{=} \int f_{T|Y,Z}(t\mid y,z)\,\Pi_{\varphi(Y,Z)}(dy,dz)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the three statements separately.

\@startsection{paragraph}{4}{\z@}{1.5ex plus
   0.5ex minus .2ex}{-1em}{\normalsize\bfseries}{(i) Lipschitz convergence.}

                
 
   
                    
       
                      
   

By the Kantorovich--Rubinstein dual representation of the Wasserstein distance, we have that for every Lipschitz function $f$

$$
\left|
\int f\,dQ-\int f\,dP
\right|
\leq
\operatorname{Lip}(f)\mathcal W_1(Q,P).
$$

By assumption, $x\mapsto r_n(x,z)$
is $b_n$-Lipschitz uniformly on $z, y$. Therefore, for any $z, y$, we have that


\begin{align*}
\left|
\mathbb E[r_n(\widetilde X'_n,z, y)]
-
\mathbb E[r_n(X,z, y)]
\right|
&\leq
b_n(z, y)\mathcal W_1(K_n,K)
\\
&=:
a_nb_n.
\end{align*}


                 

\@startsection{paragraph}{4}{\z@}{1.5ex plus
   0.5ex minus .2ex}{-1em}{\normalsize\bfseries}{(ii) Uniform convergence.} Fix $z$ and $y$. Since $
\sup_x|r_n(x,z, y)|\leq b_n(z, y),
$
we have
$
\|r_n(\cdot,z, y)\|_\infty\leq b_n.
$

Total variation gives
$$
\left|
\int f\,dQ-\int f\,dP
\right|
\leq
2\|f\|_\infty
\mathrm d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q).
$$

Applying this to $f=r_n(,\cdot,z)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|
\mathbb E[r_n(\widetilde X'_t,z, y)]
-
\mathbb E[r_n(X,z, y)]
\right|
&\leq
2b_n(z, y)\mathrm d_{\mathrm{TV}}(K_n, K)
\\
&=
2a_nb_n(z, y).
\end{aligned}
$$


\@startsection{paragraph}{4}{\z@}{1.5ex plus
   0.5ex minus .2ex}{-1em}{\normalsize\bfseries}{(iii) $L_2$ convergence.} the chi-squared divergence $\mathrm d_{\chi^2}$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm d_{\chi^2}(P\Vert Q)
:=
\left(
\int
\left(
\frac{dP}{dQ}-1
\right)^2dQ
\right)^{1/2},
\qquad P\ll Q.
$$

Suppose that $
K_n\ll K
$ and let $(X, Z, Y)$ sampled from $P_\star(X, Z, Y)$ and $(\widetilde{X}', Z, Y)$ from $P_n(\widetilde{X}', Z, Y)$. Denote by

$$
D_n(x,z, y)
:=\frac{dP_n(\widetilde{X}', Z, Y)}{dP_\star(X, Z, Y)}(x, z, y)=
\frac{dK_n(\,\cdot\mid z)}
     {dK(\,\cdot\mid z)}(x),
$$
the Radon-Nikodym derivative.

Then $\mathbb E_{K_n}[r_n]
=
\mathbb E_{K}[D_nr_n].
$ Therefore, we have that,

$$
\mathbb E_{P_\star}[r_n]-\mathbb E_{P_n}[r_n]
=
\mathbb E_{P_\star}[(D_n-1)r_n].
$$

By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and the total expectation law, we obtain that


\begin{align*}
\left|
\mathbb E_{P_t}[r_n]-\mathbb E_{P_\star}[r_n]
\right|
&\leq
\left(
\mathbb E_{P_\star}\left[(D_t-1)^2\right]
\right)^{1/2}
\left(
\mathbb E_{P_\star}\left[r_n^2\right]
\right)^{1/2}
\\
&\leq
\left(
\mathbb E_{P_\star(Z)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{K}\left[(D_t-1)^2\right]\right]
\right)^{1/2}
\left(
\mathbb E_{P_\star}[r_n^2]
\right)^{1/2}
\\
&=
\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm d_{\chi^2}(K_n\Vert K)^2\right]}
\,
\|r_n\|_{L_2}.
\end{align*}

By assumption, $\|r_n\|_{L_2}
\leq b_n.$ Hence, we conclude that

$$
\left|
\mathbb E_{P_t}[r_n]-\mathbb E_{P_\star}[r_n]
\right|
\leq
a_nb_n.
$$

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $n$ and condition on $\mathcal F_{n-1}$, $Z_n$ and $Y_n$. Note that under the null, $
X_n\mid Z_n,Y_n,\mathcal F_{n-1}
\sim
K(\cdot\mid Z_n),
$
because $X_n\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_n\mid Z_n$. By construction, we have that 
$
\widetilde X_n\mid Z_n,Y_n,\mathcal F_{n-1}
\sim
K_n(\cdot\mid Z_n).
$

Therefore, we have that
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E
\left[
E_n
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right]=
1+\lambda
\mathbb E_{K}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(X,Z_n),Y_n)
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right]
-\lambda
\mathbb E_{K_n}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(\widetilde X_n,Z_n),Y_n)
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right].
\end{align*}

Introduce the $X$-independent reference quantity $l_0(Z_n,Y_n):=l(m_0(Z_n),Y_n).$ Hence it has exactly the same value under $K$ and $K_n$, and therefore cancels from the difference. Thus
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E &
\left[
E_n
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right]-1
\\&=
\lambda
\Bigg[
\mathbb E_{K}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(X,Z_n),Y_n)-l_0(Z_n,Y_n)
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right]
-
\mathbb E_{K_n}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(\widetilde X_n,Z_n),Y_n)-l_0(Z_n,Y_n)
\mid
\mathcal F_{n-1},Z_n,Y_n
\right]
\Bigg].
\end{align*}

The expression in braces is precisely the difference between the expectations of the model-dependent component of the loss under the true and estimated conditional distributions. By Proposition~\ref{prop:double_robust}, on the corresponding good event $A_n$,
$$
\left|
\mathbb E_{K}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(X,Z_n),Y_n)-l_0(Z_n,Y_n)
\right]
-
\mathbb E_{K_n}
\left[
l(\widehat m_n(\widetilde X_n,Z_n),Y_n)-l_0(Z_n,Y_n)
\right]
\right|
\leq
a_nb_n.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\mathbb E[E_t\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]
\leq
1+\lambda a_nb_n.
$$

Thus, setting

$$
\epsilon_n:=\lambda a_nb_n,
$$

the process $(E_t)_{t\geq1}$ is an approximate e-process in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:approx_e_process}, with one-step inflation $\epsilon_n$.

We can therefore apply Proposition~\ref{prop:approx_e_type_I}. This gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P
\left(
\sup_{1\leq n\leq N}
E^{(n)}
\geq \frac{1}{\alpha}
\right)
\leq
\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_n
+
\alpha
\exp\left(
\sum_{n=1}^N\epsilon_n
\right)
=
\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_n
+
\alpha
\exp\left(
\lambda\sum_{n=1}^Na_nb_n
\right).
\end{align*}
Subtracting $\alpha$ from both sides yields
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P
\left(
\sup_{1\leq n\leq N}
E^{(n)}
\geq \frac{1}{\alpha}
\right)
-\alpha
&\leq
\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_n
+
\alpha
\left[
\exp\left(
\lambda\sum_{n=1}^Na_nb_n
\right)-1
\right].
\end{align*}

title: Setup
body_md:
Parameters are chosen by grid search ($\lambda\in[-0.99,0.99]$, $M\in(0,10]$) on a separate
pretraining sample of size $50{,}000$ and evaluated on an independent sample of size $n=20{,}000$. We report
the e-power as mean over 10 seeds, for
correct guesses $\hat\beta=\beta$, wrong-magnitude guesses and a wrong-signed guess ($\kappa<0$). Results are in
Table~\ref{tab:derandomization} and Figure~\ref{fig:derandomization}.
